A 60-year-old man is to undergo posterior fossa surgery in the sitting position. Which of the following is the MOST sensitive means of detecting venous air embolism (VAE)?
description:
VAE occurs when air is entrained into open veins in the presence of negative intraluminal pressures (i.e., negative with respect to atmospheric pressure). During posterior fossa surgery performed with the patient in the sitting position, VAE is common.

The most sensitive means of diagnosing VAE is the TEE; the least sensitive is the esophageal stethoscope.

About 10% to 30% of patients having posterior fossa surgery in the sitting position will have evidence of VAE using end-tidal CO₂ monitoring, 40% using precordial Doppler monitoring, and 50% to 100% using TEE monitoring.

Because the safety of using TEE for prolonged surgery in patients with neck flexion in the sitting position is not well established, many clinicians use the precordial Doppler to monitor for significant VAE. The precordial Doppler is currently the standard of care for VAE monitoring.

Question: When intracranial hypertension exists, the main initial compensatory mechanism from the body is

options.name: Increased absorption of CSF in the spinal arachnoid villi
Shifting of CSF from intracranial to spinal subarachnoid space
Reduction of cerebral blood volume (CBV) due to compression of intracranial arteries

description:
• Intracranial pressure is determined by the pressure contribution of three volume compartments: Brain parenchyma 80% to 90%, CSF 5% to 10%, and blood 5% to 10%.
  • Under normal circumstances, ICP is maintained within the normal range (5-15 mm Hg) over a wide range of intracranial volumes (ICVs) due to the following three compensatory mechanisms:

translocation of CSF from the intracranial to spinal subarachnoid space (this is the main initial compensatory mechanism);

translocation of intracranial blood (primarily venous) to systemic circulation;

reabsorption of CSF across arachnoid villi into the dural venous sinus and, ultimately, into systemic circulation.

CSF production is fairly constant (0.35-0.40 mL/min) regardless of ICP.

Question: Administration of vecuronium during spinal surgery may interfere with monitoring of
description:
Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) involve repetitive stimulation of the extremity and monitoring the signals at the level of the scalp. SSEPs are used to monitor the dorsal columns of the spinal cord. As this area is sensory, neuromuscular blockers such as vecuronium do not affect SSEP monitoring.

Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) monitoring is used to monitor corticospinal tracts (motor pathways) that are not assessed with SSEPs. Neuromuscular blockers, such as vecuronium, interfere with MEP monitoring and should not be used.

Question: Patients can be safely imaged in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner with conventional versions of which of the following monitors?

options.name: Pulmonary artery catheter with cardiac output probe

description:
Arterial lines do not pose a problem in the scanner because no wires come into contact with the patient. A long section of nonmagnetic fluid-filled tubing from the arterial catheter (or a CVP catheter) passes through a small channel in the wall of the MRI room to the MRI control room, where the transducer (which contains metallic parts) can be connected to a monitor.

Pulmonary artery catheters and urinary catheters with temperature wires embedded in them cannot be used in patients undergoing MRI scanning.

Standard conventional pulse oximeters and ECG wires are also unacceptable because they have ferromagnetic wires.

Question: What is the minimum quantity of intracardiac air that can be detected by a precordial Doppler?
description:
Except for the transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), the Doppler ultrasound is the most sensitive device for detection of intracardiac air.

Under ideal circumstances, as little as 0.25 mL of intracardiac air can be detected by a precordial Doppler ultrasound transducer placed over the right side of the heart.

In contrast, TEE can detect even smaller volumes of intracardiac air.

The amount of air needed to cause clinically significant VAE is much greater than that detected by Doppler or TEE (e.g., 50 mL has been aspirated from a right-sided catheter in patients who have had hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, and other ECG changes).

Question: Which of the following drugs at high doses CANNOT produce an isoelectric electroencephalogram (EEG)?
description:
Even at high doses, dexmedetomidine, ketamine, benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, midazolam), and opioids (e.g., alfentanil, fentanyl, remifentanil) cannot produce an isoelectric EEG.

At high doses, barbiturates (thiopental, methohexital, pentobarbital), etomidate, propofol, and volatile anesthetics (e.g., desflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane) can produce an isoelectric EEG.

Question: Which of the following statements is FALSE concerning cerebral blood flow (CBF)?

options.name: CBF is 10% to 20% of the cardiac output during the first 6 months of life
CBF peaks at 55% of the cardiac output between 2 and 4 years of age
CBF decreases to 35% of the cardiac output at 10 years of age

description:
CBF is coupled with cerebral metabolic rate (CMR).

CBF is 10% to 20% of the cardiac output at birth to 6 months of life, peaks at 55% of the cardiac output between 2 and 4 years of age (CBF values > 100 mL/100 g brain tissue/min), and then settles to adult values of 15% of the cardiac output by 7 to 8 years of age (CBF values of 50 mL/100 g brain tissue/min). The statement that it decreases to 35% at 10 years is FALSE.

Question: At what level of cerebral blood flow (CBF) does the EEG start to show signs of cerebral ischemia?
description:
Critical CBF is the CBF below which EEG evidence of cerebral ischemia begins to appear (EEG slowing).

Normal CBF is 50 mL/100 g brain tissue/min.

Cerebral ischemia starts to appear when the CBF falls to 20 mL/100 g brain tissue/min.

At 15 mL/100 g brain tissue/min, the EEG becomes isoelectric.

Below 15 mL/100 g brain tissue/min, membrane failure and neuronal death may develop with time.

Question: What effect does cerebral ischemia have on CBF autoregulation?

options.name: CBF autoregulation is abolished and becomes passively dependent on CPP
CBF autoregulation is ablated at low CPPs but remains intact at high CPPs
CBF autoregulation is ablated at high CPPs but remains intact at low CPPs
The CBF autoregulatory curve is shifted to the right

description:
CBF autoregulation is easily impaired and modified by numerous factors, such as cerebral vasodilators (including nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, calcium channel blockers, hydralazine, volatile anesthetics), severe hypercapnia, inflammation, traumatic brain injury (TBI), intracranial surgery, chronic hypertension, and cerebral ischemia.

Cerebral ischemia abolishes CBF autoregulation, with CBF becoming passively dependent on the CPP.

Question: Which of the following is the MOST rapid maneuver available for lowering ICP in a patient with a large intracranial mass?
description:
Ways to decrease ICP include elevating the head, hyperventilation, avoiding constriction around the neck, avoiding PEEP and excessive airway pressures, CSF drainage, hyperosmolar solutions, diuretics, IV anesthetics (e.g., propofol), and surgery.

Hypocarbia (associated with hyperventilation) will rapidly cause vasoconstriction, thereby reducing CBF, CBV, and ICP. Hyperventilation is the technique that will most rapidly decrease ICP in patients with an intracranial mass. Remember that lowering the CO₂ content will also reduce CBF and that if the blood flow is low enough, it can cause cerebral ischemia.

Mannitol (0.25-2 g/kg) can decrease brain swelling, but it can cause a transient increase in ICP due to vasodilation of the cerebral blood vessels. Because of this transient increase in ICP, mannitol is not used unless other methods to decrease brain volume and ICP have been considered.

Steroids have a dramatic effect on reducing the swelling and can decrease ICP, but the process takes hours.

Furosemide reduces CSF formation and decreases ICP.

Question: What effect does propofol have on the CO2 responsiveness of the cerebral vasculature?

options.name: Propofol attenuates the effect of hypocarbia on CBF
Propofol attenuates the effect of hypercarbia on CBF
Propofol augments the effect of hypocarbia on CBF
Propofol does not affect CO2 reactivity at a dose used clinically

description:
The cerebrovascular response to changes in PaCO₂ is preserved after the administration of propofol, as well as with other IV anesthetics (barbiturates, etomidate, and ketamine), even at doses that produce burst suppression on the EEG.

The elevated ICP can be reduced by hyperventilation in patients anesthetized with IV anesthetics.

CO₂ responsiveness is also preserved with volatile anesthetics at clinical levels of anesthesia. At high concentrations of volatile anesthetics and lower BPs, CO₂ reactivity is attenuated.

Question: Cerebral autoregulation is MOST likely to remain intact

options.name: In a patient with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3
With total IV anesthesia (TIVA) anesthetic using propofol

description:
Cerebral autoregulation can be impaired under certain conditions, including acute ischemia, inflammation, brain tumors, arteriovenous malformations, subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), intracranial surgery, and traumatic brain injury (TBI).

Volatile anesthetics above 1 minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) impair cerebral autoregulation; however, in low doses (i.e., below 1 MAC), autoregulation is maintained.

TIVA with propofol does not impair cerebral autoregulation.

Question: A 72-year-old patient undergoing resection of an astrocytoma in the sitting position suddenly develops hypotension. Air is heard on the precordial Doppler ultrasound. Each of the following therapeutic maneuvers to treat VAE is appropriate EXCEPT
description:
• The general approach to treating patients following VAE is: (1) stop further air entrainment, (2) aspirate entrained air, (3) prevent expansion of existing air, and (4) support cardiovascular function.

Cessation of subsequent air entrainment is achieved by flooding the surgical field with irrigation fluid. Additionally, neck veins can be compressed as a means of increasing jugular venous pressure, which mitigates or prevents further air entry.

To prevent expansion of the VAE, nitrous oxide is immediately discontinued.

Cardiovascular function is supported using inotropes, vasopressors, and IV fluids as indicated.

PEEP is the least correct answer. Approximately 20% to 30% of humans have a probe patent foramen ovale. Initiation of PEEP may increase the risk of paradoxical embolism or decrease venous effluent from the calvarium, resulting in increased CBV and ICP.

Question: Which of the following is the LEAST likely sequela of venous air embolism (VAE) during posterior fossa surgery in the upright position?
description:
VAE occurs when air enters the venous circulation and travels to the right atrium, where it continues into the right ventricle and passes into the lungs, causing an increase in pulmonary dead space, impairment of gas exchange (e.g., decreased oxygen absorption and CO₂ retention), and a decrease in end-tidal CO₂.

Air in the pulmonary arteries can increase pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressures (not hypotension) and can cause right heart strain and dysrhythmias.

Air can also pass right to left through a patent foramen ovale (20%-30% of patients) and may lead to stroke.

Reflex bronchoconstriction may be caused by microvascular bubbles and by the release of inflammatory mediators from endothelial cells, resulting in hypoxemia.

Initially, VAE can cause systemic hypertension, but as larger amounts of air are entrained, systemic hypotension and death from cardiovascular collapse can result.

Question: A 30-year-old anxious patient is to undergo Electrocorticography (ECoG) monitoring to identify epileptogenic foci during seizure surgery. All of the following drugs may make it easier to identify the epileptogenic foci EXCEPT?
description:
For general anesthesia and ECoG monitoring, a common anesthetic includes propofol and a muscle relaxant for induction and endotracheal intubation, followed by maintenance anesthesia with low concentrations of sevoflurane, isoflurane, or desflurane with nitrous oxide.

After about 20 to 30 minutes to lower the concentrations of the volatile anesthetic, ECoG monitoring is begun.

If there is difficulty in finding the seizure location, remifentanil, alfentanil, methohexital, or etomidate can be used to promote epileptiform discharge.

Dexmedetomidine is not known to promote epileptiform discharge and may make it harder to identify epileptogenic foci.

Question: How long after a stroke should surgery be deferred for an elective surgical procedure?
description:
At least three months after stroke, and if possible 9 to 12 months, to reduce the risk of recurrent stroke.

For patients with a history of ischemic stroke, the significant risks of recurrent perioperative stroke and death should be discussed with the patient and the surgeon, along with the risks associated with delaying surgery.

Question: A 13-year-old boy is anesthetized with a propofol infusion and remifentanil infusion for scoliosis repair. SSEP monitoring is conducted during the procedure. Which of the following structures is NOT involved in conveyance of the stimulus from the posterior tibial nerve to the cerebral cortex?

options.name: Ipsilateral dorsal column of the spinal cord

description:
SSEPs are used to monitor peripheral sensory nerve pathway function. The impulse elicited by electrical stimulation of a peripheral nerve ascends the ipsilateral dorsal column of the spinal cord, then synapses in the dorsal column nuclei at the cervicomedullary junction; these fibers cross and travel through the contralateral medial lemniscus to the thalamus, which then projects the sensory impulses to the sensory cortex contralateral to the side of stimulation.

SSEPs do not evaluate the integrity of the ventral or lateral spinothalamic tracts or the corticospinal tract (which is a motor pathway).

Question: A 75-year-old patient is undergoing craniotomy for resection of a large astrocytoma. During administration of isoflurane anesthesia, BP is 110/80 and the arterial blood gas sampling reveals a PaCO2 of 30 mm Hg. At this time, this patient's global CBF would be approximately
description:
Arterial CO₂ tension (PaCO₂) has a profound physiologic effect on CBF and CBV.

At the normal PaCO₂ of 40 mm Hg, CBF is 50 mL per 100 g brain tissue per minute.

Between PaCO₂ values of 20 and 40 mm Hg, CBF decreases 1 to 2 mL per 100 g of brain tissue per min for each 1 mm Hg decrease in PaCO₂ from a PaCO₂ of 40 mm Hg.

Because this patient's PaCO₂ is 10 mm Hg below normal (40-30 = 10), CBF would be decreased 10 to 20 mL to approximately 30 to 40 mL per 100 g of brain tissue per min (approximately 35 mL).

Question: A 24-year-old patient is brought to the ICU after sustaining a closed head injury in a motor vehicle accident. Each of the following would be useful in managing intracranial hypertension in this patient EXCEPT

options.name: Hyperventilation to a PaCO2 of 35 mm Hg

description:
Studies evaluating the effectiveness of corticosteroids in the setting of head injury, or global or focal brain ischemia, have demonstrated either no improvement or a worsening of neurologic outcome. The use of steroids is not recommended.

Propofol is recommended to help control ICP.

Hyperventilation is recommended as a temporizing measure for the reduction of elevated ICP. The target PaCO₂ is 35 to 45 mmHg.

Hyperosmolar therapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline may lower intracranial pressure.

Question: A 30-year-old patient with a spontaneous SAH from a ruptured intracranial aneurysm is to undergo surgery. This patient does not have signs of concomitant cerebral vasospasm. Preoperative treatment may include any of the following EXCEPT
description:
After an SAH, patients may experience cerebral vasospasm (25% of patients) as well as rebleeding, intracranial hypertension, and seizures.

If the patient is NOT experiencing cerebral vasospasm, hypertension should be avoided to minimize aneurysmal wall tension, thereby mitigating the risk of re-rupture and further hemorrhage. In contrast, had this patient been experiencing cerebral vasospasm, induced hypertension would have been an appropriate therapeutic intervention.

Narcotics and benzodiazepines may be cautiously administered to reduce pain and anxiety (sedation).

Antiepileptic drugs often are administered in an attempt to prevent or mitigate seizures.

Calcium channel blockers (e.g., nimodipine) are used to avert adverse sequelae of cerebral vasospasm.

Question: Which of the following frequency ranges is seen on the EEG in the normal awake patient?
description:
The EEG records the electrical activity of the brain. When evaluating the EEG, one looks at the frequency, the amplitude, and the location of the leads on the head.

The usual awake patient has a frequency on the beta range (high frequency and low amplitude) common with that of the alert patient.

With eye closure, the frequency of the EEG is in the alpha frequency (slower but with higher amplitude).

When slower frequencies are produced (theta and delta), the brain is depressed.

Question: A 75-year-old patient with signs and symptoms of an SAH is brought to the emergency room for evaluation. T-wave inversion, a prolongation of the QT interval, and U waves are noted on the preoperative ECG. Appropriate action at this point would be to
description:
SAH is associated with ECG changes (> 40% of patients) that are largely reversible and felt to be related to localized catecholamine stimulation in response to the bleeding. ECG changes include T-wave inversion, prolonged QT interval (often > 550 msec), and appearance of U waves.

Electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., hypokalemia or hypocalcemia) may contribute to the etiology of the ECG changes, so it would probably be most appropriate to quantify these electrolytes before initiating other therapies or canceling emergency surgery.

Nitroglycerin is a potent cerebral vasodilator that could have a deleterious effect on ICP in patients with increased ICP.

There is no evidence that the administration of β-blockers (e.g., esmolol, metoprolol) alters the outcome of these patients.

Although a pulmonary artery catheter is sometimes placed in patients with cardiac disease, a patient with an SAH does not need one, because the problem is neurogenic and not cardiac in origin.

Question: An alcoholic 62-year-old male patient is noted to have jaundice one day after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy under halothane/fentanyl general endotracheal anesthesia. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase are elevated, but alanine aminotransferase (serum glutamic–pyruvic transaminase [SGPT]) and aspartate aminotransferase (serum glutamic–oxaloacetic transaminase [SGOT]) are within normal ranges. Of note, all values were within normal limits in this patient preoperatively. The most likely cause of his jaundice is

An initial bolus of pancuronium was administered to a patient with end-stage liver disease with associated ascites for general anesthesia. Appropriate anesthetic considerations include all of the following, except

options.name: Larger volume of distribution requiring initial larger doses
Longer duration of action requiring smaller maintenance doses

description:
Chronic liver disease may interfere with the metabolism of drugs due to decreased number of functional hepatocytes or decreased hepatic blood flow that typically accompanies cirrhosis of the liver.

Cirrhotic patients will require a larger initial dose of pancuronium due to increased volume of distribution for this hydrophilic agent with smaller maintenance doses for prolonged duration of action.

Pancuronium has slight vagolytic activity resulting in increased heart rate and cardiac output (increased sympathomimetic activity).

Pancuronium does not cause intense histamine release.

Question: A chronic alcoholic patient with liver cirrhosis is likely to demonstrate all of the following during administration of anesthesia, except

options.name: A high minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) for desflurane
Resistance to the hypnotic effects of thiopental
Resistance to the analgesic effects of opiates

description:
Opioid hyperalgesia is not a typical finding in this specific clinical context compared to the other options.

Chronic alcohol consumption is a well-documented factor that increases the Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics like desflurane (high MAC).

Chronic alcoholics often exhibit resistance to intravenous induction agents like thiopental (increased volume of distribution and cross-tolerance at the GABA receptor level).

Due to chronic alcohol-induced changes in neurotransmitter systems and potential cross-tolerance at opioid receptors, these patients often require higher doses of opioids to achieve effective analgesia (resistance to analgesic effects of opiates).

Question: A woman with long-standing alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Turcotte Pugh B) presents to the emergency room for chronic shortness of breath and abdominal pain. A review of her lab findings reveal a hematocrit concentration of 36% (hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL) with an arterial blood gas revealing a PaO2 of 65 mm Hg breathing a FIO2 of 0.5 via face mask. Her vitals are a blood pressure of 135/60 mm Hg and a heart rate of 88 bpm. The most likely cause of her hypoxemia is
description: Those with chronic liver disease are at increased risk of arterial venous shunting. The presence of intrapulmonary shunting will result in hypoxemia.

Question: Which of the following cardiovascular abnormalities is least likely to be present in a patient with end-stage alcoholic cirrhosis?
description:
Cirrhosis is typically associated with several cardiovascular abnormalities including a hyperdynamic circulation characterized by increased cardiac output and decreased peripheral resistance.

Other cardiovascular changes include a resting tachycardia, warm peripheries, a bounding pulse, and a widened pulse pressure.

Increased peripheral vascular resistance is the least likely to be present (peripheral resistance is typically decreased).

Question: A patient with chronic liver disease is scheduled for a laparoscopic abdominal operation. The risk of mortality during surgery for this patient is assessed using
description:
The Child-Turcotte-Pugh score is used to predict mortality during surgery in patients with chronic liver disease, namely, cirrhosis.

The Mayo or model for end-stage liver disease (MELD) was initially developed to predict death within 3 months of surgery in patients who had undergone a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure and was subsequently found to be useful in determining prognosis and prioritizing patients for liver transplant.

Alvarado score is used for appendicitis, while the Ranson criteria assess pancreatitis.

Question: The variable not used to calculate a MELD (model for end-stage liver disease) score to prioritize patients for liver transplantation is
description:
• The MELD score is a formulaic calculation utilizing three variables: creatinine, INR, and bilirubin.

For dialysis-dependent patients, the creatinine score is automatically set to 4 mg/dL despite true serum levels.

Albumin is NOT used to calculate the MELD score.

Question: A patient presents for preoperative evaluation for upcoming surgery. He has a history of liver transplantation 2 years ago, otherwise feeling well. Which of the following is most likely to be present during preoperative evaluation?
description: Long-standing insufficient liver function is believed to cause changes in the circulation that changes vessel tone and blood flow in the kidneys. The likely presence of renal insufficiency (elevated serum creatinine) is a consequence of these changes in blood flow, rather than direct damage to the kidney itself.

Question: During laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the risk of failure to visualize contrast material entering the duodenum during intraoperative cholangiogram is highest with the administration of
description:
μ-Receptor agonism may contribute to sphincter of Oddi spasm, preventing passage of contrast. Full μ-agonists (like morphine) are more likely to contribute versus partial μ-agonists (e.g., buprenorphine) and agonist–antagonist (e.g., nalbuphine).

Naloxone, as a μ-antagonist, would alleviate any opioid-induced spasm.

Question: Drugs that can decrease or reduce opioid-induced biliary spasm include all of the following, except
description:
A variety of agents that can produce smooth-muscle relaxation have been used. Nitrates and calcium channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem) have been the most extensively studied.

Anticholinergics, including atropine and glucagon, are additional agents that can provide sphincter of Oddi relaxation.

Metoclopramide is a promotility agent that enhances sphincter smooth muscle contraction (it increases spasm, does not decrease it).

Question: Each of the following is associated with delayed gastric emptying, except
description:
Sympathetic celiac plexus blockade leaves parasympathetic fibers unopposed with associated increased gastrointestinal motility and possible diarrhea (not delayed gastric emptying).

Diabetes mellitus, vagotomy, and μ-receptor agonism (opioids) are all associated with delayed gastric emptying.

Question: Which of the following is considered the most sensitive indicator of impending traumatic renal failure?
description:
Impending renal failure often starts as pre-renal failure, where the kidney responds to hypovolemia/decreased renal perfusion by maximal sodium conservation, resulting in a low FENa (<1%) .

While serum creatinine is a standard marker, it is a late indicator that often rises only after substantial kidney function is lost (often taking 48-72 hours).

FENa can detect early physiological changes in renal perfusion and function before irreversible tubular injury (Acute Tubular Necrosis - ATN) occurs, making it a better indicator of impending rather than established failure.

Question: A 26-year-old male patient with Alport syndrome requires hemodialysis (every third day) and presents for an arteriovenous fistula creation. His last dialysis treatment was yesterday. Patient requests general anesthesia for this procedure. Which of the following drugs will have a prolonged duration of action?
description:
In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage renal disease (ESRD), the elimination of many drugs is altered.

Neostigmine is primarily excreted by the kidneys (about 50-80% excreted unchanged in the urine within 24 hours), and its elimination half-life is prolonged in patients with renal failure, leading to a longer duration of action.

Question: Each of the following is associated with acute tubular necrosis, except
description:
Acute tubular necrosis is classified as a "renal" (e.g., not prerenal or postrenal) cause of acute kidney injury.

Diagnosis is made by a fractional excretion of sodium >3% , greater than expected urine sodium concentration with low osmolality, and presence of muddy casts on urinalysis.

Low urine flow, concentrated urine, or an acidic environment can contribute to the formation of hyaline casts, pointing to hypovolemia and prerenal failure (not ATN).

Question: A 67-year-old patient with chronic renal failure presents for hip arthroscopy to address and treat his labral tears and associated hip pain. The best option for opioid therapy in this patient is
description:
Fentanyl is metabolized by the liver into inactive, non-toxic metabolites and has no significant active renal excretion. Therefore, fentanyl is considered one of the safest opioids to use in patients with chronic renal failure.

Meperidine is contraindicated in renal failure because its metabolite, normeperidine, accumulates and causes neurotoxicity, including seizures.

Codeine metabolites accumulate and are known to cause profound toxicity and CNS depression in advanced renal impairment.

Dextropropoxyphene metabolites accumulate, and it is associated with CNS/cardiac toxicity.

Question: During major abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia, a sudden drop in mean arterial pressure (MAP) to 50 mmHg leads to the release of renin. Which cells in the kidney are responsible for this secretion?
description:
JG cells act as intrarenal baroreceptors that sense a drop in stretch (pressure) in the afferent arteriole. They are the primary site for the synthesis, storage, and release of renin into the circulation.

Macula densa cells are located in the distal convoluted tubule and sense changes in sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration. While they can trigger the JG cells to release renin via paracrine signaling, they do not secrete renin themselves.

Podocytes are epithelial cells of the Bowman's capsule that form the filtration slits.

Mesangial cells provide structural support to the glomerular capillaries and have contractile properties to regulate the filtration surface area.

Question: Renal blood flow (RBF) is maintained relatively constant despite fluctuations in systemic blood pressure through autoregulation. This mechanism typically operates within which range of Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)?
description:
Autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR is maintained between a MAP of approximately 80–180 mmHg in normal adults.

Outside the 80–180 mmHg range, autoregulation fails. If pressure drops too low, RBF and GFR fall sharply; if it rises too high, glomerular capillaries are directly exposed to damaging pressures.

Question: Which part of the nephron is the primary site of action for Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) to regulate water reabsorption?

options.name: Descending Limb of the Loop of Henle
Ascending Limb of the Loop of Henle

description:
Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, is the body's primary regulator of water balance.

ADH binds to V2 receptors on the cells of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and collecting duct.

This binding triggers the insertion of Aquaporin-2 water channels into the cell membranes, making the normally impermeable walls of the DCT and collecting duct highly permeable to water, allowing it to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream and concentrating the urine.

Question: Which of the following inhalational anaesthetics is most associated with potential nephrotoxicity due to the production of Compound A during its degradation in carbon dioxide absorbents?
description:
Sevoflurane is the inhalational anaesthetic most associated with the production of Compound A.

When sevoflurane reacts with strong base carbon dioxide absorbents (such as soda lime or Baralyme), particularly under low-flow conditions, it degrades to produce Compound A (fluoromethyl-2,2-difluoro-1-(trifluoromethyl)vinyl ether).

Although this compound has been shown to cause nephrotoxicity in rats, its clinical significance in humans remains debated and generally considered minor.

Question: A 68-year-old male with a history of hypertension (on Lisinopril) and moderate chronic kidney disease (CKD, baseline Cr 1.8 mg/dL) undergoes a complex 6-hour abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. Intraoperatively, he was hypotensive (MAP < 60 mmHg) for 90 minutes. Postoperatively, he is oliguric (0.2 mL/kg/hr). Which of the following mechanisms best explains the renal dysfunction?

options.name: Decreased renal cortical perfusion due to hypoperfusion

description:
Prolonged hypotension (MAP < 60 mmHg) during surgery causes significant renal ischemia. This ischemic insult causes hypoperfusion of the renal cortex, particularly in vulnerable areas, leading to acute tubular necrosis (ATN).

Reduced perfusion decreases the oxygen supply to the kidney, causing ischemia-reperfusion injury, which manifests as postoperative AKI, especially in patients with pre-existing moderate chronic kidney disease.

Question: A 50-year-old female is scheduled for a kidney transplant. The anesthesiologist needs to optimize renal perfusion and maintain hemodynamic stability. Regarding renal physiology, which of the following is true concerning the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)?

options.name: The macula densa senses increased NaCl in the distal tubule and increases renin secretion.
Renin is secreted in response to increased tubular pressure.
Juxtaglomerular cells are located in the walls of the efferent arteriole.
Renin is released in response to decreased perfusion pressure in the afferent arteriole.

description: The juxtaglomerular (JG) cells in the kidney act as high-pressure baroreceptors. When there is a decrease in perfusion pressure (blood pressure) within the afferent arteriole, these cells are stimulated to release renin into the bloodstream. This is a primary trigger for the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS).

Question: Which anesthetic technique or agent is preferred to minimize the risk of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI)?
description:
Based on clinical studies and meta-analyses, Intravenous anesthesia with propofol and remifentanil (Total Intravenous Anesthesia, or TIVA) is generally associated with a lower incidence of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) compared to volatile anesthetics (like sevoflurane or isoflurane), particularly in high-risk procedures such as cardiac, thoracic, and major abdominal surgery.

Propofol has known antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic properties, which can help protect the kidneys from ischemia-reperfusion injury.

Question: The factor associated with maximum increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) is

options.name: Increased central venous pressure to 14 mm Hg
Ventilation with positive end–expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5 cm H2O

description:
Coughing and bucking can cause a much higher increase in ICP (acute increase) than any of the other factors listed.

Between PaCO₂ values of 20 and 80 mm Hg, CBF increases by 1 mL/100 g/min and cerebral blood volume increases by 0.05 mL/110g/min per mm Hg increase in PaCO₂.

Increase in CVP and adding PEEP will minimally increase ICP by affecting venous return.

Question: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) (mm Hg) in a patient with intracranial pressure (ICP) of 12 mm Hg, central venous pressure (CVP) of 15 mm Hg, and mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 70 mm Hg will be
description:
CPP = MAP – ICP or CVP, whichever is higher.

Here, CVP (15 mm Hg) is higher than ICP (12 mm Hg).

Thus, CPP = 70 – 15 = 55 mm Hg.

Question: Treatment of a patient with mannitol can lead to all the following, except
description:
Mannitol, a six-carbon sugar, is the most commonly used diuretic in neuroanesthesia practice. It is an osmotic diuretic and undergoes little or no reabsorption. It also improves renal blood flow.

Side effects include an initial increase in circulatory volume, which can cause pulmonary edema (hypervolemia).

Diuresis attributed to mannitol can lead to hypovolemia and hypokalemia.

Mannitol causes diuresis (increased urine output), not oliguria.

Question: A patient is undergoing craniotomy for subdural hematoma. During the procedure, the surgeon requests lowering the intracranial pressure. All the following can be used, except
description:
Treatment of intracranial hypertension includes hyperventilation to PaCO₂ of 25 to 30 mm Hg, improving CSF drainage by elevating the head by 30 degrees or surgical placement of CSF drain, using an osmotic diuretic (mannitol), hypertonic saline, decompression craniectomy, and barbiturates.

Furosemide can also be used to reduce CSF formation and decrease ICP.

Corticosteroids have been used to decrease cerebral edema and take a few hours to have effect, but routine use of corticosteroids in managing intracranial hypertension is not recommended.

Question: The desired level of PaCO2 in a neurosurgical patient is
An absolute contraindication for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is
description: Contraindications to ECT include pheochromocytoma, recent myocardial infarction (<3 months), recent stroke, intracranial mass or increased ICP, angina, poorly controlled heart failure, significant pulmonary disease, bone fractures, severe osteoporosis, pregnancy, glaucoma, and retinal detachment.

Question: Signs of air embolism in a patient include all, except
description: Clinical signs of venous air embolism include a decrease in end tidal CO₂, a decrease in arterial oxygen saturation, sudden hypotension (not hypertension), mill wheel murmur, and even sudden circulatory arrest.

Question: A 65-year-old male is undergoing surgery for medulloblastoma in the posterior fossa of brain. Approximately 1 hour into surgery you notice arrhythmias on the monitors. The next step will be
description:
For posterior fossa tumor resection, the patient is frequently placed in the sitting or prone position.

Operations on posterior fossa tumors can injure vital brain-stem respiratory and circulatory nuclei, resulting in hemodynamic fluctuations or depression of ventilation.

The surgeon should be informed at the first sign of cardiac arrhythmias.

Question: Nitrous oxide should be avoided in patients with
description:
Nitrous oxide can diffuse into closed air spaces, which may be of significant clinical consequences. The blood/gas coefficient of nitrous oxide is 0.47, whereas that of nitrogen is 0.015. This means that nitrous oxide is about 33 times more diffusible than nitrogen.

Nitrous oxide can quickly expand closed gas spaces, such as middle ear or a pneumothorax or pneumocephalus.

Question: The following fluid should be avoided in a patient undergoing craniotomy
description:
In a patient undergoing craniotomy, intravenous fluid replacement should be performed by using glucose-free isotonic crystalloid or colloid solutions.

Hyperglycemia is known to worsen ischemic brain injury. Therefore, Dextrose 5%—normal saline (which contains glucose) should be avoided.

Question: Best measure to reduce cerebral oxygen consumption includes
description:
Hypothermia is one of the most effective methods for protecting the brain against ischemia.

Hypothermia decreases both basal and electrical metabolic requirements throughout the brain, unlike intravenous anesthetic agents or hyperventilation.

Question: A patient with spinal injury, sustained 3 hours ago, comes to the OR for exploratory laparotomy. Anesthetic management of the patient includes which of the following?
description:
In the early management of acute spinal injury patients, particular emphasis should be placed on preventing further spinal damage, which may occur during patient movement, airway manipulation, and positioning.

High-dose corticosteroids are often administered to help improve neurological outcome.

Patients with high cord transections may have impaired airway reflexes, hypotension, and bradycardia and may be prone to hypothermia.

Succinylcholine can be used safely in first 24 hours following spinal injury (risk of hyperkalemia begins after 24-48 hours).

Question: Anesthetic management of a patient with multiple sclerosis (MS) includes

options.name: Use of succinylcholine can result in hypokalemia

description:
MS is characterized by progressive demyelination in the brain and spinal cord.

Stress, anesthesia, and surgery can have detrimental effects on the course of the disease.

Succinylcholine should be avoided to prevent hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia).

Hyperthermia should be avoided as an increase in temperature may block nerve conduction.

Advanced MS may be associated with autonomic dysfunction.

Question: True statement about autonomic hyperreflexia is

options.name: Lesions below T10 is responsible for the reflex
It can be treated with deep general anesthetic
It is associated with vasoconstriction above the site of injury
It can be provoked by thermal stimulation

description:
Autonomic hyperreflexia is seen in patients with spinal cord injury at or above T6.

It is characterized by acute generalized sympathetic hyperactivity in response to a triggering stimulus (most commonly distension of hollow viscera - bowel or bladder).

Clinical signs include severe hypertension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, profuse sweating, vasodilation above the level of lesion, and pallor and vasoconstriction below the level of lesion.

Deep general anesthesia has been used in preventing autonomic hyperreflexia.

Question: True statement about cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is

options.name: It is formed in the third ventricle
It is absorbed in arachnoid granulations present in fourth ventricle
Total volume of CSF is about 150 mL
Major mechanism of formation is by passive diffusion of ions

description:
CSF is formed by the choroid plexuses of the lateral ventricles.

In adults, normal CSF production is about 20 mL/hour with a total volume of about 150 mL.

The CSF is absorbed in arachnoid granulations over cerebral hemispheres.

CSF formation involves active secretion of sodium in the choroid plexuses, and not passive diffusion.

Question: The only inhalational anesthetic that can cause an isoelectric EEG among the following is
description:
Isoflurane can produce an isoelectric EEG at 2 to 2.5 MAC.

Enflurane typically produces a spike and wave pattern at 2 to 3 MAC. Seizure activity may be seen on EEG with 3% enflurane in a hypocapnic patient.

Halothane causes slowing of EEG activity with increasing concentration until 4 MAC, after which it produces uniform activity.

Increasing sevoflurane concentration from 2 to 5 MAC changes the cortical EEG pattern from a high-amplitude slow wave to burst suppression to an isoelectric EEG interspersed with spikes.

Question: All the following are relative contraindications to a sitting craniotomy, except
description:
The incidence of venous air embolism in sitting craniotomies is about 20% to 40%.

The presence of right-to-left shunt can cause paradoxical air embolism. Air embolism can have catastrophic consequences, such as coronary ischemia and stroke.

Thus, sitting position should be avoided in patients with a right-to-left shunt, patent foramen ovale, or ventriculoatrial shunt.

Ventriculoperitoneal shunt is not a contraindication to sitting craniotomy.

Question: Signs and symptoms of raised intracranial hypertension include all the following, except
description:
Increased intracranial pressure (ICP) can lead to altered mental status, intractable vomiting, and focal or global neurological deficits.

Clinical signs include hypertension, bradycardia (not tachycardia), irregular respiration, and pupillary changes (papilledema may be seen on fundoscopy).

Cushing triad consists of raised ICP, hypertension, and bradycardia.

Question: Etomidate in a dose of 0.2 mg/kg can lead to all the following, except

options.name: Increase amplitude and latency of somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs)

description:
Etomidate decreases cerebral metabolic rate, CBF, leading to a decrease in intracranial pressure.

It enhances SSEP.

It is a sedative hypnotic but lacks analgesic properties.

Ventilation is affected to a lesser extent with etomidate when compared to barbiturates or benzodiazepines. Induction doses usually do not result in apnea, and it does not abolish the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide.

Question: The relationship between PaCO₂ and cerebral blood flow is:
description:
The relationship between PaCO₂ and CBF is linear between PaCO₂ 20–80 mmHg.

Between a PaCO₂ of 20 and 80 mm Hg, CBF changes approximately 1 to 2 mL/100 g/min per mm Hg change in PaCO₂.

Question: At PaCO₂ levels below 20 mmHg, the CBF curve:
description:
At PaCO₂ levels below 20 mmHg, the CBF curve plateaus due to maximal vasoconstriction.

CO₂ gas tension has the greatest influence on cerebral blood flow (CBF).

Question: Therapy for cerebral vasospasm includes
description:
Therapies for cerebral vasospasm include "triple-H therapy" (hypertension/hypervolemia/hemodilution) , balloon angioplasty, and intra-arterial nicardipine and other vasodilators.

Cerebral vasospasm usually develops 3 to 14 days post-subarachnoid hemorrhage, resulting in narrowing of cerebral blood vessels and decreased blood flow distally.

Question: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of asthma?

options.name: Chronic inflammatory changes in the submucosa of the airways

description:
Asthma is a type of reactive airway disease characterized by hyperresponsive airways, reversible expiratory airflow obstruction, and chronic inflammation.

Elastase deficiency in the airways is a feature of emphysema.

Question: A 55-year-old male presented to you with a pulmonary function test report, which shows an increase of FEV1 percent predicted of more than 12%, and an increase in FEV1 of greater than 0.2 L in response to bronchodilators. Which characteristic of his respiratory illness is depicted here?

options.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)—variability in airflow obstruction

description:
Response to a bronchodilator drug resulting in relief of airway obstruction is highly suggestive of bronchial asthma.

A more than 12% increase in predicted FEV₁ and an absolute increase in FEV₁ of more than 0.2 L suggest acute bronchodilator responsiveness and variability in airflow obstruction.

The reversibility of this magnitude is almost always indicative of bronchial asthma. COPD patients do respond to bronchodilators but not to the same extent.

Question: Which of the following techniques is associated with a lower complication rate related to bronchospasm in the asthmatic population?
description:
In a severely asthmatic patient, regional anesthesia is superior to general anesthesia with an LMA, which is better than general anesthesia with ETT.

The choice of anesthetic technique is often influenced by the severity of asthma, history of previous intubations for asthma, dependence on inhaled bronchodilators, and patient preference.

The goal in any such circumstance is to decrease airway manipulation and stimulation.

Question: A 22-year-old patient with a history of moderate persistent asthma on medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting inhaled β-agonist presents for an emergency appendectomy. On clinical examination, he is actively wheezing, but maintaining an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Which of the following statements about this clinical scenario is most appropriate?

options.name: Presence of wheezing on physical examination indicates that he is having a severe attack of asthma
Volatile anesthetics cause bronchodilation through catecholamine-independent mechanisms
Increased airway resistance that occurs intraoperatively is usually due to acute exacerbation of asthma
A laryngeal mask airway (LMA) is more stimulating to the airway than an endotracheal tube, and should be avoided in asthmatics

description:
Volatile anesthetics are potent bronchodilators, and they act through catecholamine-independent mechanisms. They are rarely used as second-line agents in cases of bronchospasm refractory to medical therapy.

History and physical examination can suggest presence of severe asthma if the patient has had repeated intubations for asthma. Even though high-pitched, musical wheezes are characteristic of asthma, they are not specific and they have no correlation with the severity of obstruction.

Mechanical causes of obstruction such as a kinked endotracheal tube or a mucous plug can also present a similar clinical picture and are more common.

General anesthesia through LMA is less stimulating to the airway than through an endotracheal tube.

Question: Which of the following changes in lung volumes and mechanics occurs during induction of general anesthesia?
description:
• Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) Reduction: Induction of general anesthesia consistently causes a decrease in FRC, often described as a reduction of 15-20% or about 0.4-0.5 liters. This is primarily due to the loss of diaphragmatic muscle tone, leading to a more cephalad (upward) position of the diaphragm.

Closing capacity usually remains unchanged or may be reached earlier, but the reduction in FRC often causes the FRC to drop below the closing capacity, causing dependent airway closure and atelectasis.

Thoracic/respiratory system compliance generally decreases, not increases, during anesthesia.

Question: What is the primary mechanism for the rapid development of atelectasis and subsequent shunt during general anesthesia?
description:
High inspired oxygen concentrations (often used during preoxygenation or maintenance) wash out nitrogen from the alveoli. Since oxygen is rapidly absorbed into the bloodstream and nitrogen is not present to hold the alveoli open, the alveoli collapse, a process known as absorption atelectasis.

This occurs most frequently in dependent lung regions when anesthesia reduces the functional residual capacity to below the closing capacity, causing airway closure and trapping of the oxygen-rich gas.

This rapid absorption and collapse lead to intrapulmonary shunting.

Question: A 20-year-old man involved in a motor vehicle accident is brought to the operating room for irrigation and debridement of open fractures of the femur and humerus. Cyanosis, decreased breath sounds on the left, increased peak airway pressure, and hypotension are noted after intubation of the trachea. The most likely cause is
description:
• Tension Pneumothorax: In trauma, positive-pressure ventilation can convert a simple pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax. Air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, causing intrapleural pressure to exceed atmospheric pressure. This leads to collapse of the ipsilateral lung (causing decreased breath sounds), shifts the mediastinum to the contralateral side, and compresses the great vessels. The resulting decrease in venous return to the heart causes hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. The high pressure required to ventilate the resisting chest cavity explains the increased peak airway pressure.
  • Intubation of the Right Mainstem Bronchus: While this would cause decreased breath sounds on the left and increased airway pressures, it typically does not cause hypotension.
  • Fat Embolus: Fat embolism syndrome typically presents over 24–72 hours with a triad of respiratory distress, neurological changes, and a petechial rash.
  • Aspiration: While aspiration can cause hypoxia and increased airway pressures, it is less likely to cause immediate, severe hypotension.

Question: A woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is extubated and minimally responsive after isoflurane anesthesia. She is receiving oxygen 6 L/min through a face mask. Respirations are 10/min, PaO2 is 68 mmHg, PaCO2 is 54 mmHg, and pH is 7.28. The most likely cause of the respiratory acidemia is

options.name: blunted sensitivity to low pH in the medullary respiratory center
depression of carotid body chemoreceptors by halothane

description:
The most likely cause of her respiratory acidemia is depression of carotid body chemoreceptors by residual volatile anesthetic (halothane/isoflurane).

Potent volatile anesthetics significantly blunt the hypoxic ventilatory drive. This occurs because these agents depress the peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies.

In a patient with COPD, who may already have a decreased sensitivity to CO₂ and rely more heavily on their "hypoxic drive" to breathe, even low (sub-anesthetic) concentrations of residual gas can cause significant respiratory depression and subsequent acidemia.

Question: The sudden onset of pulmonary edema can be caused by each of the following EXCEPT

options.name: rapid re-expansion of the lungs following pneumothorax

description:
• Oxygen toxicity: While high concentrations of oxygen can cause lung damage (absorption atelectasis or tracheobronchitis), this typically occurs after prolonged exposure (usually >24–48 hours) . It does not manifest as a sudden onset of pulmonary edema.
  • Rapid re-expansion of the lungs: This can lead to re-expansion pulmonary edema (REPE) , a rare but serious complication that occurs immediately after a collapsed lung is quickly re-inflated.
  • Upper airway obstruction: This causes Negative Pressure Pulmonary Edema (NPPE) . Intense inspiratory efforts against a closed airway create significant negative intrathoracic pressure, drawing fluid into the alveoli.
  • Rupture of mitral papillary muscle: This causes acute, severe mitral regurgitation, leading to a sudden backflow of blood and pressure into the lungs, resulting in immediate pulmonary edema.

Question: The carbon dioxide/ventilation response curve

options.name: is primarily a measure of the integrity of the peripheral chemoreceptors
shows parallel displacement to the left in the presence of opioids
is linear between a PaCO2 of 20 and 120 mmHg
shows progressive changes in slope with increased doses of halogenated anesthetics

description:
• Shows progressive changes in slope with increased doses of halogenated anesthetics: Volatile agent dose-dependently depress the slope (reduce ventilatory response to CO₂).

The CO₂/ventilation response curve primarily reflects central chemoreceptor sensitivity (medulla responding to CO₂ via CSF pH), not peripheral chemoreceptors.

Opioids cause a rightward shift with decreased slope (reduced sensitivity + increased apneic threshold).

The relationship is approximately linear only in a limited physiological range (~40–80 mmHg), not across such extremes (20-120 mmHg).

Question: Measurement of which of the following provides the most reliable information about the severity of bronchospasm?
description:
To assess severity of bronchospasm, you want a parameter that best reflects airflow limitation (especially expiratory flow).

Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV₁) directly measures the degree of airflow obstruction. It falls significantly in bronchospasm (as in asthma) and is widely used clinically to grade severity.

Diffusing capacity (DLCO) reflects gas transfer across alveoli, not airway narrowing.

Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is a lung volume; changes are nonspecific and not sensitive to airway obstruction.

Residual volume (RV) increases due to air trapping but is indirect and less reliable than flow measurements.

Question: When compared with a healthy 30-year-old man, which of the following respiratory parameters is decreased in an otherwise healthy 80-year-old man?

options.name: Ratio of functional residual capacity to total lung capacity

description:
Resting tidal volume decreases with age — elderly individuals tend to have shallower breathing with compensatory ↑ respiratory rate.

Alveolar–arterial (A–a) O₂ gradient increases with age due to V/Q mismatch.

Lung compliance increases with age (loss of elastic recoil of lung tissue).

Ratio of FRC to TLC increases with age (↑ FRC due to air trapping; TLC relatively unchanged).

Question: A 35-kg child requires mechanical ventilation with pure oxygen at a tidal volume of 350 ml and a rate of 20/min during a severe asthma attack. The most likely cause of severe hypotension after initiating mechanical ventilation is
description:
• In a severe asthma attack, the airways are narrow and obstructed. When mechanical ventilation begins, the following cycle occurs: Air Trapping → Breath Stacking → Increased Intrathoracic Pressure → Reduced Venous Return → Low Cardiac Output → Hypotension.

The leading cause of this is inadequate expiratory time leading to "Dynamic Hyperinflation."

The patient is receiving 100% (pure) oxygen, so hypoxic depression is unlikely.

Respiratory alkalosis causes shifts in electrolytes but rarely acute hypotension.

Question: Which of the following pulmonary components is altered the most in a morbidly obese patient?
description:
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) is altered the most in morbidly obese patients.

ERV decreases exponentially as Body Mass Index (BMI) increases. It is considered the most sensitive indicator of the respiratory effects of obesity.

The sharp drop in ERV is the primary driver behind the characteristic reduction in Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) seen in obesity.

Question: Addition of 20 cmH2O positive end-expiratory pressure to a patient receiving controlled mechanical ventilation decreases cardiac output and left ventricular function by
description:
The addition of 20 cmH₂O positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) primarily decreases cardiac output and left ventricular function by increasing right ventricular afterload.

High levels of PEEP (typically >15 cmH₂O) cause alveolar compression, which compresses the adjacent pulmonary capillaries, leading to a rise in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). The right ventricle (RV) must work harder to pump blood against this increased resistance (increased afterload). As RV afterload increases, the RV may dilate, causing the interventricular septum to bulge into the left ventricle (LV), reducing LV filling (decreased preload) and leading to a fall in stroke volume and cardiac output.

Question: A 95-kg, 65-year-old woman receives sevoflurane and pancuronium during a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Three minutes after administration of neostigmine 5 mg and atropine 1.2 mg, the twitch height returns to normal. Spontaneous tidal volume is 500 ml when the endotracheal tube is removed. In the PACU she reports dyspnea and appears distressed. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the respiratory distress?
description: The most likely cause of the respiratory distress is residual muscle paralysis (or residual neuromuscular blockade). Although twitch height returned, 3 minutes is generally considered inadequate time for full reversal of a long-acting muscle relaxant like pancuronium, especially given the rapid reversal attempt.

Question: During application of continuous positive airway pressure, lung compliance increases because of
description:
• Decreased lung water: Reducing extravascular lung water relieves pulmonary congestion. Stiff lungs caused by edema become more distensible (compliant) as the fluid is cleared.
  • Decreased airway resistance: While CPAP can help keep airways open (stenting), airway resistance refers to the friction of airflow rather than the elasticity of the lung tissue (compliance) itself.
  • Decreased venous return: CPAP actually decreases venous return as a side effect due to increased intrathoracic pressure. However, this typically leads to a decrease in cardiac output, not an increase in lung compliance.
  • Increased intercostal muscle tone: CPAP generally reduces the work of breathing and respiratory muscle activity rather than increasing muscle tone.

Question: During anesthesia, the ventilation/perfusion ratios change

options.name: to preferential ventilation of the dependent portion
due to cephalad shift of the diaphragm
by insignificant amounts from that in the awake state
to preferential perfusion of the superior portion

description:
During anesthesia, the ventilation/perfusion ratios change due to cephalad shift of the diaphragm.

  • During general anesthesia (with or without paralysis): Loss of diaphragmatic tone allows the abdominal contents to push the diaphragm toward the head (cephalad shift), especially in the dependent regions. This reduces resting lung volume (FRC), leading to airway closure and atelectasis in the dependent portions of the lung. While perfusion remains preferential to the dependent regions due to gravity, ventilation shifts away from these collapsed areas toward the non-dependent (superior) regions, creating a significant ventilation/perfusion mismatch.

Question: Static lung compliance is decreased by each of the following EXCEPT
description:
Pulmonary emphysema is a classic obstructive lung disease characterized by loss of elastic recoil, which actually increases static lung compliance (the lungs become easier to inflate, not harder).

ARDS causes widespread alveolar collapse, inflammation, and loss of functional surfactant, making the lungs very stiff and significantly decreasing static compliance.

Pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease where healthy lung tissue is replaced by stiff, scarred connective tissue, making the lungs difficult to expand, resulting in a profound decrease in static compliance.

Inhalational anesthesia typically causes a decrease in static compliance, primarily due to the development of atelectasis (collapsed alveoli) in dependent lung regions.

Question: Carbon dioxide retention first occurs when the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to vital capacity (FEV1/VC) decreases below
description:
Carbon dioxide retention in obstructive lung disease appears late, when airflow limitation becomes severe.

  • Mild–moderate obstruction: FEV₁/VC falls but PaCO₂ remains normal (patient compensates by increasing ventilation).
  • Severe obstruction: alveolar hypoventilation develops → CO₂ retention begins.

Clinically, this tends to occur when FEV₁/VC falls below ~50% .
